Exposure Lens Singapore: Technical Appendix

Reproducible spatial analysis behind the HD4 prototype dashboard

Genie Tang

30 September 2026, 04:29 UTC (document generation time)

Contents

  • Purpose
  • Data
  • Choice of spatial statistics
  • Spatial autocorrelation of air temperature
  • Local indicators of spatial association (LISA)
  • Maps

  • Session information

This list is written out in full instead of left as an automatic Word table of contents field, so it always shows the section names, in every viewer and every export, without needing a manual field refresh.

Purpose

This document is the reproducible companion to the interactive “Exposure Lens Singapore” dashboard, built as a discussion prototype for HD4. This is an independent prototype built for that discussion; it is not a formal HD4 deliverable or output. The dashboard is an interactive prototype; this appendix shows the underlying data, the exact statistical methods available at this scale, and states plainly which methods are not yet valid at this scale. Nothing here is polished past what the data supports.

Two dates matter here, and they are not the same thing. The date at the top of this document (next to the title) is when this HTML file was generated, that is, when this script was last run. The date below is when the underlying air quality and temperature readings were actually observed. Air quality changes hour to hour, so if you re-run this script on a later day without updating the numbers, the generation date will move forward but the observation date will not, and the two will visibly disagree. That disagreement is a signal to go pull fresh numbers, not a bug.

The readings below are saved observations from a live pull of Singapore’s data.gov.sg real-time API (National Environment Agency), not a live, auto-refreshing feed: this document reports a fixed snapshot, and re-running it later reproduces the same snapshot instead of fetching new numbers. This is a public API: no account, application, or credentials are required to call it.

  • PM2.5 endpoint: https://api-open.data.gov.sg/v2/real-time/api/pm25
  • Air temperature endpoint: https://api-open.data.gov.sg/v2/real-time/api/air-temperature
  • Observation time: 2026-09-19, 13:00 SGT (read from the API response itself, not assumed)
  • Retrieved: 2026-09-19, during this project’s build

Both endpoints accept a date= parameter to pull a different day’s readings; changing it does not change what is written into this script, since the numbers below are typed in instead of fetched at render time (see Data, next).

Data

The two tables below are typed into this script, so this file is fully self-contained and does not make a network call when rendered. No external data files are needed to run it. Because the values are typed in instead of fetched live, they are exactly reproducible, but they will not update automatically if you re-run this script tomorrow; that is a deliberate trade-off for a snapshot report, not an oversight.

pm25 <- data.frame(

Station names above are NEA’s official names, matching the data workbook. The two static maps later in this appendix label each point with its station ID instead, since eighteen full station names would not fit legibly at that scale.

Choice of spatial statistics

Two different geometries are in play, and they should not be confused with each other.

NEA’s five air-quality reporting regions (North, South, East, West, Central) are reported as single values per region, not as measured boundaries. Five is not disqualifying by itself; there is no universal minimum sample size that makes Moran’s I mathematically invalid. The actual problem is more specific, and worth demonstrating instead of asserting:

pm_pts <- st_as_sf(pm25, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
pm_proj <- st_transform(pm_pts, 3414)
pm_coords <- st_coordinates(pm_proj)
nb_pm <- suppressWarnings(knn2nb(knearneigh(pm_coords, k = 4)))
lw_pm <- nb2listw(nb_pm, style = "W")
mt_pm <- suppressWarnings(moran.test(pm25$value, lw_pm))

With five regions and the same “four nearest neighbours” rule used below for temperature, each region ends up connected to all four of the others: the neighbour graph is fully connected. Under row-standardised weights, a fully connected graph on n units forces Moran’s I to exactly -1/(n-1), regardless of what the data actually are. Here that is -0.25, and the computed value confirms it:

Computed Moran’s I for the PM2.5 regions under this weighting: -0.25, identical to -1/(n-1) to the third decimal place. R itself warns that the test is degenerate here (“out-of-range p-value: reconsider test arguments”). That is not a coincidence of these particular numbers; it is a property of the weighting choice colliding with having only five units, and it means Moran’s I under this fully connected weighting structure would not provide information about spatial pattern in the observed values, no matter which five values were plugged in. The deeper issue behind this is that NEA’s reporting regions are label points for broad zones, not measured locations with an agreed neighbour structure, so there is no principled way to define “nearest neighbours” for them in the first place. Both problems point the same way: cluster statistics are left out for the PM2.5 regions on purpose, not because a five-observation rule forbids them.

NEA’s 18 air-temperature stations, in contrast, are individually geolocated point observations with real coordinates, so a neighbour structure can be defined without guessing. Eighteen points is still a small sample, but it is large enough to demonstrate the method well, with the standard caveat that any single test at this sample size is illustrative. It is not a validated finding.

The rest of this appendix runs a real Moran’s I test on the temperature network, using four-nearest-neighbour (k = 4) weights based on projected distance, since polygon boundaries are not required for point data.

Spatial autocorrelation of air temperature

The question this section asks: do temperature readings at nearby stations tend to be more similar to each other than readings at far-apart stations would be, more than chance alone would produce?

pts <- st_as_sf(temp, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
pts_proj <- st_transform(pts, 3414)
coords <- st_coordinates(pts_proj)

nb <- knn2nb(knearneigh(coords, k = 4))
lw <- nb2listw(nb, style = "W")

moran_result <- moran.test(pts$value, lw)
moran_result
## 
##  Moran I test under randomisation
## 
## data:  pts$value  
## weights: lw    
## 
## Moran I statistic standard deviate = 3.1354, p-value = 0.0008582
## alternative hypothesis: greater
## sample estimates:
## Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
##        0.38379340       -0.05882353        0.01992873

The neighbour rule is precise, and worth stating exactly instead of calling it “distance-based”: each station is linked to its four nearest neighbours, each of those four links weighted equally at one quarter. Distance is used only to choose which four stations count as neighbours; once chosen, all four get the same weight regardless of how near or far they are within that group of four. This graph is also directional: station A can list station B as one of its four nearest neighbours without B necessarily listing A back, since “nearest four” is evaluated independently at each station. That is a normal property of nearest-neighbour graphs, not an error, but it means the weights matrix is not symmetric.

The distance to a station’s fourth-nearest neighbour ranges from 7.7 to 15.5 km across the network. These are broad station-to-station relationships across the island, not street-scale thermal conditions, and the result below should be read at that scale.

Analytical result. The analytical test above reports Moran’s I = 0.384, with an analytical p-value of 0.000858. That analytical p-value relies on a normal-approximation assumption that is more reliable with larger samples; at 18 stations, a permutation test is the more defensible primary result.

set.seed(20260919)
moran_perm <- moran.mc(pts$value, lw, nsim = 9999)
moran_perm
## 
##  Monte-Carlo simulation of Moran I
## 
## data:  pts$value 
## weights: lw  
## number of simulations + 1: 10000 
## 
## statistic = 0.38379, observed rank = 9950, p-value = 0.005
## alternative hypothesis: greater

Permutation result (primary). Across 18 stations with four-nearest-neighbour weights, Moran’s I is 0.384, with a one-sided permutation p-value (testing for positive spatial autocorrelation) of 0.005 based on 9,999 random permutations of the station values across the fixed locations. This is weaker evidence than the analytical p-value of 0.000858 suggests, but it still supports a real positive spatial pattern: stations resemble their nearest neighbours more than a random relabelling of the same 18 values would, more often than chance would produce. A permutation p-value is itself simulation-based, so re-running with a different random seed or simulation count will move this figure slightly; treat it as “about 0.005,” not as a fixed constant.

How sensitive is this to the choice of four neighbours? Re-running the same test with each station linked to its three, five, and six nearest neighbours instead of four checks whether “four” was a convenient choice that happens to produce a significant result:

Sensitivity of the result to the neighbour-count choice
Nearest neighbours (k) Moran’s I Permutation p-value
3 0.392 0.0068
4 0.384 0.005
5 0.341 0.0044
6 0.328 0.0035

Moran’s I stays in a narrow band (roughly 0.328 to 0.392) and the permutation p-value stays below 0.01 across every choice from three to six neighbours. That supports the snapshot finding being reasonably insensitive to this particular modelling choice; it does not, on its own, explain what is physically producing the pattern (see the closing section below).

This result supports a specific, limited claim: temperature readings across the 18 stations reporting in this snapshot show positive spatial autocorrelation at the observation time above, under the neighbour definition stated here. It is offered as a worked demonstration of method at a small sample size, not as a validated finding about Singapore’s temperature climatology in general.

Local indicators of spatial association (LISA)

The question this section asks: which individual stations show a value similar to their nearest neighbours (a locally consistent reading), and which show a value unlike their neighbours (a local contrast)? “High” and “low” below are always relative to this snapshot’s own station mean (32.29 degrees C), not a health or comfort threshold.

local_analytic <- localmoran(pts$value, lw, alternative = "two.sided")
set.seed(20260919)
# alternative = "two.sided" (spdep's default) and sample_Ei = TRUE (also the
# default) together select the resampling this appendix reports. The
# permutation itself draws each simulated neighbour value with replacement
# from the other stations' observed values (spdep's default
# no_repeat_in_row = FALSE); it is not a without-replacement shuffle.
local_perm <- localmoran_perm(pts$value, lw, nsim = 9999, iseed = 20260919,
                               alternative = "two.sided")

p_perm_col <- "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"
# spdep's localmoran_perm() returns more than one permutation-based p-value.
# "Pr(folded) Sim" is a folded [0, 0.5] rank statistic that needs doubling
# before it is on the standard [0, 1] scale Benjamini-Hochberg expects.
# "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim" is the two-sided rank-based permutation p-value
# spdep computes on that [0, 1] scale for the alternative
# requested above, so it is used here as is, without any doubling. The two
# routes are close but not identical, since they rank the simulated
# reference distribution slightly differently, particularly with tied
# values; using the column spdep itself labels for a two-sided test avoids
# that ambiguity instead of reconstructing an equivalent by hand.
p_perm_twosided <- local_perm[, p_perm_col]
p_analytic_bh <- p.adjust(local_analytic[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"], method = "BH")
p_perm_bh <- p.adjust(p_perm_twosided, method = "BH")

# Quadrant classification: compare each station's own value, and the average
# of its four neighbours' values, against the network mean. This describes
# the local pattern (self vs. neighbours); it is not itself a significance
# test, which is why it is reported alongside, not instead of, the p-values.
z <- pts$value - mean(pts$value)
wz <- lag.listw(lw, pts$value) - mean(pts$value)
pattern <- ifelse(z >= 0 & wz >= 0, "High-High",
            ifelse(z < 0 & wz < 0, "Low-Low",
            ifelse(z >= 0 & wz < 0, "High-Low", "Low-High")))

lisa_table <- data.frame(
  station = temp$name,
  station_id = temp$id,
  temperature_c = temp$value,
  local_moran_i = round(local_analytic[, "Ii"], 3),
  pattern = pattern,
  permutation_p = round(p_perm_twosided, 4),
  permutation_p_bh = round(p_perm_bh, 4)
)
ft_table(lisa_table[order(-lisa_table$local_moran_i), ],
         widths = c(2.5, 0.45, 0.8, 0.7, 0.7, 0.75, 1.0),
         header_labels = c(station = "Station", station_id = "ID",
                            temperature_c = "Temperature (°C)",
                            local_moran_i = "Local Moran's I",
                            pattern = "Local pattern",
                            permutation_p = "Permutation p",
                            permutation_p_bh = "Permutation p, BH-adjusted"),
         caption = "Local Moran's I by station, four-nearest-neighbour weights")

With 18 stations tested at once, some individually small p-values are expected by chance alone; that is exactly what a multiple-testing adjustment checks for. After a Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment across all 18 stations, no station remains significant at the conventional 0.05 threshold (the smallest adjusted p-value is 0.231 using the permutation-based local p-values, and 0.154 using the analytical ones). The “local pattern” column above (High-High, Low-Low, High-Low, Low-High) describes each station’s relationship to its own neighbours in this snapshot, for example Semakau Island, Jurong Island, and Sentosa all sit in the Low-Low quadrant (a relatively cool reading surrounded by relatively cool neighbours), and East Coast Park sits in Low-High (a relatively cool reading surrounded by relatively warm neighbours). None of these individual station patterns should be read as a confirmed local cluster or hotspot after the adjustment above; they describe this snapshot’s pattern, not a statistically established one.

Maps

The two maps below use the identical color ramps and equal-size-marker convention as the interactive dashboard, so that this static appendix and the interactive page read as one consistent picture of the same data, instead of two different-looking versions of it. A subdued land outline (OpenStreetMap land polygons at 100-metre resolution, which include Sentosa, Jurong Island, Pulau Ubin and the other offshore islands where several stations sit) is added below for geographic orientation, with Singapore drawn darker than the facing coasts of Johor and the Riau Islands, along with a north arrow and a scale bar sized to the map’s own longitude at Singapore’s latitude, drawn in an area of open water clear of every station and region marker. Neither map uses planning-area or NEA region boundary polygons: URA’s planning-area polygons are publicly available, but the NEA reporting-region geometry that would match these five PM2.5 values has not been established for this prototype (see the dashboard’s stated scope). Point locations and color are both real; there is no interpolation between points and no implied boundary. The color domain on each map is computed from the data actually plotted, not fixed in advance, so a future re-run with a wider or narrower range of values will always color across its own full range instead of silently clipping at an old domain.

pm25_ramp <- colorRampPalette(c("#9cc9e0", "#74add1", "#4a8bbd", "#286e9b", "#104667"))(101)
pm25_domain <- range(pm25$value)
pm25_idx <- pmax(1, pmin(101, round((pm25$value - pm25_domain[1]) / diff(pm25_domain) * 100) + 1))

# Contrast-aware label color: dark circles get white text, light circles get
# dark text, instead of one fixed color that goes unreadable on part of the
# ramp (the darkest circle, Central at 141, was unreadable with dark text).
label_col_pm25 <- vapply(pm25_ramp[pm25_idx], function(hex) {
  rgb_val <- col2rgb(hex)
  lum <- 0.299 * rgb_val[1] + 0.587 * rgb_val[2] + 0.114 * rgb_val[3]
  if (lum < 140) "white" else "#173d44"
}, character(1))

xr <- c(103.60, 104.05)
yr <- c(1.15, 1.48)

par(mar = c(7, 4, 2, 1), pty = "s")
plot(pm25$lon, pm25$lat, type = "n", xlim = xr, ylim = yr, asp = 1,
     xlab = "Longitude (°E)", ylab = "Latitude (°N)",
     main = "PM2.5 by reporting region")
grid(col = "#e5e5e5", lty = 1)
draw_land()
points(pm25$lon, pm25$lat, pch = 21, bg = pm25_ramp[pm25_idx], col = "#173d44", lwd = 1.5, cex = 5.5)
text(pm25$lon, pm25$lat, labels = paste0(pm25$name, "\n", pm25$value),
     cex = 0.68, font = 2, col = label_col_pm25)
box()
legend("bottomleft", legend = c(pm25_domain[1], round(mean(pm25_domain)), pm25_domain[2]),
       pt.bg = pm25_ramp[c(1, 51, 101)], pch = 21, title = "µg/m³", bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
draw_north_arrow(cx = 103.995, cy = 1.445, height = 0.026)
draw_scale_bar(x0 = 103.865, y0 = 1.178, total_km = 10, lat_for_scale = 1.3, seg_km = 5)
mtext("Circles mark NEA's reporting-region label points, not boundaries or extent.",
      side = 1, line = 4.2, cex = 0.65, col = "#666666")
mtext("19 Sept 2026, 13:00 SGT. Source: data.gov.sg (NEA). Land: OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL).",
      side = 1, line = 5.4, cex = 0.65, col = "#666666")

All five regions fall inside NEA’s official “Elevated” 1-hour PM2.5 band (56 to 150 µg/m³). The roughly two-fold spread from North (71) to Central (141) is a real pattern in this snapshot, but with five regional reporting values represented by NEA label points, under a degenerate neighbour structure (see above), it is a descriptive observation, not a tested spatial cluster.

temp_ramp <- colorRampPalette(c("#eec3a0", "#e2a985", "#c96f4f", "#a8402e", "#7a1f1f"))(101)
temp_domain <- range(temp$value)
temp_idx <- pmax(1, pmin(101, round((temp$value - temp_domain[1]) / diff(temp_domain) * 100) + 1))

par(mar = c(7, 4, 2, 1), pty = "s")
plot(temp$lon, temp$lat, type = "n", xlim = xr, ylim = yr, asp = 1,
     xlab = "Longitude (°E)", ylab = "Latitude (°N)",
     main = "Air temperature by station")
grid(col = "#e5e5e5", lty = 1)
draw_land()
points(temp$lon, temp$lat, pch = 21, bg = temp_ramp[temp_idx], col = "#78352b", lwd = 1.2, cex = 2.2)
text(temp$lon, temp$lat, labels = temp$id, cex = 0.55, font = 2, pos = 3, offset = 0.35, col = "#3a2117")
box()
legend("bottomleft", legend = c(sprintf("%.1f", temp_domain[1]), sprintf("%.1f", mean(temp_domain)), sprintf("%.1f", temp_domain[2])),
       pt.bg = temp_ramp[c(1, 51, 101)], pch = 21, title = "°C", bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
draw_north_arrow(cx = 103.995, cy = 1.445, height = 0.026)
draw_scale_bar(x0 = 103.865, y0 = 1.178, total_km = 10, lat_for_scale = 1.3, seg_km = 5)
mtext("Station IDs match the tables above. No interpolation shown.",
      side = 1, line = 4.2, cex = 0.65, col = "#666666")

Limitations

This appendix demonstrates working competence with the actual statistical toolkit named in the dashboard: sf for spatial data handling and projection to Singapore’s SVY21 metric system (EPSG:3414), and spdep for Moran’s I and LISA, including permutation-based inference and a multiple-testing correction.

The temperature result supports a specific, bounded claim: the 18 stations reporting in this snapshot show positive spatial autocorrelation in air temperature, at that observation time, under the stated neighbour definition, and that result holds up under a permutation test and across a range of nearby neighbour-count choices. It does not establish persistent heat hotspots, personal exposure, an urban heat-island effect, or any effect of building design; a single snapshot cannot distinguish a built-environment signal from coastal setting, station siting, local weather at that hour, or other causes. Establishing any of those would need repeated observations over time, not a single 13:00 SGT reading.

More generally, this appendix does not establish a validated exposure-clustering finding for Singapore, because:

  1. The PM2.5 data has only five NEA reporting regions, represented as point locations, not polygons. The same four-nearest-neighbour rule used for temperature, applied to only five regions, connects each region to all four of the others, so the resulting graph is fully connected. Under equal weights, that specific fully connected graph forces a mathematically degenerate result at that count regardless of the values. The 18-station temperature network uses the same rule but is not fully connected, since each station links to only four of the other seventeen, which is why this problem does not apply to the temperature result. A different neighbour definition might avoid the PM2.5 problem, but choosing one only to produce a number would not be a principled analysis on its own.
  2. The temperature network is large enough to demonstrate the method well, but it is still a small sample by the standards of a full spatial epidemiology study. It reflects one snapshot in time, not a temporal series.
  3. The NEA reporting-region boundary geometry corresponding to these five PM2.5 values has not been established for this prototype. URA planning-area polygons are publicly available, but they represent a different geographic system and cannot simply be substituted for the NEA reporting regions, so no true polygon-adjacency analysis (as opposed to four-nearest-neighbour weights based on projected distance) has been run.

Access to HD4’s finer-grained SG100K and environmental-exposure data, together with spatial units appropriate to those data, would let this same pipeline run at a more meaningful spatial resolution. It would not, on its own, validate the pipeline: validation would additionally require a justified spatial relationship for the unit in question, repeated observations over time, measurement checks, and, for any health linkage, an appropriate exposure model and its own separate methodological and data-access review. This appendix is an independent prototype built for discussion with HD4, not a claim of formal affiliation with it or a substitute for that further work.
